The first thing that arrives is not an idea but a hum—the low electric murmur of a mind pretending it isn’t waiting. Somewhere behind the sentence, a door opens onto a hallway of other sentences, most of them unfinished. I think about how strange it is to be asked for words without a subject, as though someone handed me a jar and said, “Fill it with air.” The jar is the constraint. The air is whatever the room is made of. So here is the room: a desk, a window with rain on it, a cup that has gone cold, and the sense that somewhere a clock is doing its patient arithmetic.

I used to believe writing began with an idea. Now I suspect it begins with attention. You look at a thing long enough and it becomes odd. A spoon on a table is not just a spoon; it is a small silver boat beached on a white shore, carrying the memory of soup. A chair is a question about posture. A window is a negotiation between inside and outside, and the rain is the sound of that negotiation failing politely. If you spend enough time describing the ordinary, it starts to leak meaning. That leak is probably what people call imagination.

There is a street I remember from childhood, though I am not sure it existed exactly as I remember it. It sloped downhill toward a bakery, and the bakery had a sign with a loaf of bread painted on it—a loaf so idealized it looked like a cloud wearing a belt. On summer evenings the street smelled of warm asphalt and yeast, and the light came sideways and turned the dust into gold. I have carried that street around for years. It is more real to me than some places I have actually visited twice. Memory is not a filing cabinet. It is a theater company that keeps restaging the same play with new actors, sometimes badly, sometimes with such conviction that you weep.

I wonder whether every person has a private map made of such streets. Not the cartographer’s map, with its coordinates and its careful blue rivers, but the other one: the map of where you learned to ride a bicycle, where a dog once barked at you through a fence, where you waited in the dark for someone who was late and felt the evening grow heavier with each passing car. That map has no scale. A block can contain a decade. A kitchen table can be a continent.

The rain outside is doing what rain does: making the world look slightly underwater. The window is beaded with drops, and each drop holds a tiny upside-down version of the street—a compressed world, curved and silver. I like the idea that every drop is a lens. It suggests that perspective is not a luxury but a condition of seeing at all. Move an inch and the picture changes. Move a mile and you are in someone else’s weather.

I have been thinking lately about the phrase “the middle of nowhere.” It is a strange phrase, because nowhere must have a middle if it has edges, and no one agrees where those edges are. Maybe the middle of nowhere is simply the place where your phone stops buzzing and the sky becomes large again. Or the place where a road keeps going though no one asked it to. There is a kind of honesty in landscapes that don’t care whether you find them beautiful. A field is a field. A mountain is a mountain. They do not perform. They simply continue, which is one definition of dignity.

If I were to write a letter to the future, I would not include predictions. I would include instructions for paying attention. Notice the way light collects in a glass. Notice the sound a book makes when it closes. Notice how anger is often fear wearing a heavier coat. Notice that most people are doing the best they can with the weather they were given, which is not an excuse but a reason for gentleness. Notice the way a stranger holds a door and for one second you share a small, wordless government of courtesy.

But I would also include warnings. Do not confuse speed with progress. Do not let the algorithm decide what you remember. Do not mistake the loudest voice for the wisest one. Keep a few useless things: a stone from a beach, a ticket stub, a sentence someone said that you cannot explain but cannot forget. Useless things are often the hinges on which the useful door of the self swings open.

The cup is still cold. The rain has softened into mist. Somewhere a person is laughing in a room I will never see, and the sound travels because that is what sounds do—they trespass, gently, on the privacy of distance. I think this is what writing is, in the end: a kind of trespassing with permission, a way of saying, Here is my window, here is my rain, here is the small arithmetic of my attention. You are free to look. You are free to look away. But for a moment, we are in the same room, and the jar is full of air, and the air is moving.
